extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in international affairs / diplomats / policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: A historical newspaper report covering Security Council deliberations (primarily on whether to investigate Spain/Franco), related diplomatic conferences, and wartime domestic incidents. Focuses on procedural arguments, proposals for commissions/subcommittees, and the evidentiary and jurisdictional standards discussed by delegates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient prima facie case for inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The Council should satisfy itself that 'a sufficient prima facie case has been made out justifying supplementary inquiries' before ordering further action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires factual evidence that is not 'too meager'; used as the threshold justification for supplementary inquiries or for appointing a commission (as argued by the Australian delegate and others). Delegates warned action should be evidence-based rather than speculative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic jurisdiction / non-intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: Situations 'essentially within the domestic jurisdiction' of a country should not automatically be treated as matters for the Security Council to take action on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some delegates argued the Spanish question was essentially a domestic matter; this principle affects whether the Council should investigate or intervene. Balancing respect for sovereignty vs international peace implications is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invocation of Article 35 of the Charter
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of Article 35 as a procedural basis for Council consideration: to declare that a situation 'has led to international friction and endangers international peace and security' and thereby justify Council action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolutions and proposed actions should be 'in accordance with Article 35' and the Charter; wording of resolutions must align with Charter provisions to be procedurally proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unanimity / consensus for Council action
rubrics_metrics.description: A preference among delegates for unanimous conclusions or broad agreement before adopting measures or resolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegates stressed the value of unanimity and of resolutions being 'acceptable and satisfactory' to members; proposals and amendments were more likely to be supported if they could obtain broad consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission / subcommittee mandate: verify facts and report
rubrics_metrics.description: A commission or subcommittee should be appointed to 'make further studies' and to determine/verify facts (for example, presence of Nazis in Spain or whether aggression occurred) and to report details to the Council.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals included appointing subcommittees of five members to study evidence and prepare draft recommendations or resolutions. The commission's duties should include fact-finding, verification, and preparation of recommendations consistent with the Council's competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance evidence quality against danger of delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Delegates debated that while delay in inquiry can increase danger to peace, action should not be taken without adequate evidence—i.e., urgency must be weighed against evidentiary sufficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some argued that proposed committee delay was 'in no sense dangerous' while others warned delay could be 'fatal'; decision-makers must weigh the immediate risk to peace against whether available information is adequate to justify measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of Council competence and careful wording
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals and committee mandates must respect the competence of the Security Council and avoid extraneous or extramural actions beyond its remit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegates cautioned against wording or actions that might present matters 'to the detriment of' the Council or that would improperly broaden its scope; amendments and draft resolutions should be carefully framed to stay within Charter-prescribed powers.
